Civilization seems to be dependent on fighting wars to gain resources, or even at first, to conquer new territory for the people from small volunteer armies to large state-level organizations; slavery of course was a key structural component for larger societies that needed the teamwork from large portions of organized populations. In the Ancient Near East, before the Harley quote, you had armies of regional armies, but it’s important to note that even these regions, like the Plains of Syria and others, were part of broader (and internally divided) regional kingdoms. The Chaldean kingdom had histories of long time (and not at all neat) wars.

At some point from around 500 BCE through the 300s AD, the central governments seem to transition into colonies, perhaps characterized by rebellion against the original state-owners. to know what meat tastes best, how much to use, when to serve it, and why. But this last aspect is the hardest for me, because I have always wanted to serve food to different people without resorting to fetishes. I try not to show myself off, like those who are proud of their efforts and praise their creation, but I am always a little awed, because I sense in myself something wild, something forgotten, something out of place. A visiting friend, one of those who tell me I am unusual (and sometimes they do go into detail about what precisely makes me unusual), once said to me: "You feel that way because you're a neurobiologist. You're so intensely solvable. And the thing about food is that it incubates so perfectly; it's more psychological than physiological. You know? It has to do with the social interaction of cook and eater, the tips to avoid, and the attitude one brings to a meal."

A visiting friend, one of those who tell me I am unusual (and sometimes they do go into detail about what precisely makes me unusual), once said to me: "You feel that way because you're a neurobiologist. You're so intensely solvable. And the thing about food is that it incubates so perfectly; it's more psychological than physiological. You know? It has to do with the social interaction of cook and eater, the tips to avoid, and the attitude one brings to a meal."

In a crock pot, add the dry ingredients to the hot water, stir together to combine. Toss in the fruit pieces, apple cider vinegar and ginger.

Wild rice

Sucanat

Brown rice syrup

½ cup brown sugar

1 tablespoon cinnamon

2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar

½ tablespoon ginger

In a crock pot, add the dry ingredients to the hot water, stir together to combine. Toss in the fruit pieces, apple cider vinegar and ginger. Cook on high for 3-4 hours (adjust for your timing as needed), stirring every so often. If the fruit doesn't take on the spice of the blend, add a pinch of sugar to the stock pot water until the fruits turn a touch softer. The flavor improves as the fruit begins to decompose and any water drips off. Enjoy!



Tip: An added bonus to this recipe is that the dried apples rot, releasing more apple-y goodness into the broth as they compost.

Wild rice/ quinoa grain - To get the best flavor use white, red, black or other depths of rices that are difficult to overpower. Use a wide variety of different grains since they all differ in the degree of dryness they require. It is ok if they are formed into pastes and handled in a medium- fine sieve.

Soaked overnight - The grains should be soaked for at least 12 hours. You might think, why can't one cook quinoa the same way we cook barley for baking? Its because quinoa is water insoluble. Awakening dried cooked grains stored for a long time will remove their gelatin, and any water held in their proteins. (After you have soaked the grains and sprinkled the table salt, you will be using them in the soup' about three times as much.)

Soup' - Cooked quinoa tips make a thick and creamy topping for the finished soup.

by Guest Columnist Lindsay Gunther

Part of Elizabeth Warren’s formidable public persona is her declared lack of interest in taking campaign donations or attending fundraisers. “I haven’t been kind to the other candidates —who were more dependent on big-money donors — long before I became the subject of an MSNBC commercial,” she wrote in her memoir last year. How would she approach the race for president if she got the opportunity? Is taking a buck from a billionaire businessman-entrepreneur like Donald Trump beneath her? Or is she above making such an advance, no matter how unpalatable to her political self?
